candidate.answerReason: Every allowed number N with digit sum S satisfies 2N ≥ 21S. Equality is attained by 189, giving the minimum 189/18 = 10.5.

methods.label: Method 1: Prove a sharp lower bound
methods.explanation:
A small hundreds digit and a large units digit are promising because place value makes the hundreds digit much more costly in the numerator. The allowed number \(189\) gives
\[
\frac{189}{1+8+9}=\frac{189}{18}=10.5.
\]
We will prove that no allowed number has a smaller quotient.

Let \(a,b,c\) be the hundreds, tens, and units digits. They are distinct integers from \(1\) to \(9\). Write
\[
N=100a+10b+c,\qquad S=a+b+c>0.
\]
To compare \(N/S\) with \(10.5=21/2\), clear the positive denominator:
\[
2N-21S=179a-b-19c.
\]
We have \(a\ge1\). Also, \(b+19c\le179\): if \(c=9\), distinctness gives \(b\le8\), so \(b+19c\le8+171=179\). If \(c\le8\), then \(b+19c\le9+152=161\).

It follows that
\[
2N-21S\ge179-179=0,
\qquad \frac NS\ge\frac{21}{2}.
\]
The digits of \(189\) are distinct and nonzero, and its quotient attains this bound. Thus the minimum is \(\boxed{10.5}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses place value and a linear inequality with two elementary digit cases, followed by an attaining example.

methods.label: Method 2: Improve the digits one at a time
methods.explanation:
Let the distinct nonzero digits be \(a,b,c\), and define
\[
R(a,b,c)=\frac{100a+10b+c}{a+b+c}.
\]
For any fixed three digits, rearranging them leaves the denominator unchanged. The numerator is smallest when the digits increase from left to right: swapping a larger digit in a higher place with a smaller digit in a lower place decreases the number by the positive difference in place values times the positive difference in digits. Thus a minimum must have \(a<b<c\).

If \(a>1\), replacing it by \(1\) keeps the digits distinct. Comparing the two quotients gives
\[
R(a,b,c)-R(1,b,c)
=\frac{(a-1)(90b+99c)}{(a+b+c)(1+b+c)}>0.
\]
All factors in the denominator are positive. Therefore the minimum has \(a=1\).

With this digit fixed, rewrite the quotient as
\[
R(1,b,c)=1+\frac{99+9b}{1+b+c}.
\]
For fixed \(b\), the numerator of the fraction is positive, so increasing \(c\) decreases the quotient. Because \(1<b<c\le9\), choosing \(c=9\) is allowed and is best.

Now \(b\) ranges from \(2\) to \(8\), and
\[
R(1,b,9)=\frac{109+10b}{b+10}
=10+\frac9{b+10}.
\]
This is smallest when \(b=8\), the largest allowed value. Hence \(189\) gives the minimum
\[
10+\frac9{18}=\boxed{10.5},
\]
choice \(\text{C}\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses elementary exchange comparisons and positive-denominator fraction comparisons, without calculus.

candidate.annotationRationale: The route-neutral target is proving an attained discrete minimum. Both methods translate decimal digits into a number and its digit sum. The first route proves a universal linear bound using inequality properties. The second uses rearrangement, subtraction comparisons, and rational-expression simplification to improve candidates. Those route-specific procedures are not combined into a single requirement.

review.mathematicalCheck: Method 1 proves 2N−21S=179a−b−19c≥0 using a≥1 and the complete bound b+19c≤179; 189 attains equality. Method 2 correctly orders the digits, proves that replacing a>1 by 1 decreases the quotient, and then minimizes successively at c=9 and b=8.
review.levelCheck: Both proofs explain their decisive comparisons using accessible school algebra and positive denominators.
review.methodDistinctness: The universal sharp bound and the successive digit improvements provide distinct, useful approaches.
review.annotationCheck: The attained discrete minimum is route neutral. Shared place-value and expression-writing support is justified, while inequality and subtraction procedures remain method specific.
